--- title: "Regression or classification?" description: "The first fork in the road, and the marine responses that fit neither box cleanly." order: 1 categories: [supervised, regression, classification] --- ## The fork that fixes everything else Everything downstream follows from one question: **what kind of thing is your response?** It fixes the model family, what the algorithm is trying to minimise, which performance measures mean anything, and what the output can be used for. It is also a question people answer too quickly. "Abundance is a number, so it is regression" is right in outline and wrong in the details that matter, the details that made [section 1's polynomial model](../01-introduction/prediction-and-explanation.qmd) predict negative fish. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the Python tabs Most code blocks on this page have an **R** and a **Python** tab, and picking one switches the whole page. The R tab is what produced the tables and figures you see; the Python tab is the scikit-learn equivalent, shown for translation rather than executed by the site. Figures stay in R throughout, and a few steps with no scikit-learn counterpart have no Python tab, which is itself worth noticing. It is real code, not pseudocode: it runs against the same files through `python/mlbasic_data.py`, and `python/check-snippets.py` executes every snippet in the site to keep it honest. Expect the **numbers to differ slightly**: R and Python draw their random splits from different generators, so the split is not the same one. The conclusions are. ::: ## The idea **Regression** predicts a quantity: abundance, biomass, temperature, percentage cover. Output is a number, and being close counts for something: predicting 11 when the truth is 12 is nearly right. **Classification** predicts a category: present or absent, species A or B, habitat class. Output is a class, or better a probability for each class, and being close does not count: you are either right or wrong, though a probability of 0.48 for the wrong answer is a different kind of wrong from 0.02. That is the textbook division. Marine responses are frequently awkward: | Your response | It is | The catch | | --- | --- | --- | | Catch in kilograms | Regression | Usually skewed; often needs a log | | Counts of individuals | Regression | Discrete, non-negative, variance grows with the mean | | Counts with many zeros | Regression | Zero-inflated or hurdle models | | Presence / absence | Classification | Usually imbalanced | | Percentage cover | Regression | Bounded at 0 and 100; beta regression | | Habitat class | Classification | Often ordinal, and treating it as nominal loses the order | | Species identity from an image | Classification | Many classes, very imbalanced | | Community composition | Neither, quite | Compositional; parts sum to one | Ordinary linear regression assumes the response is unbounded and continuous with constant variance. Almost nothing in that table satisfies that. ## Worked example Our survey measured one thing, how many individuals were caught at each station, and it supports both framings. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey |> summarise( stations = n(), mean_count = round(mean(abundance), 2), variance = round(var(abundance), 2), zeros = sum(abundance == 0), zero_pct = round(100 * mean(abundance == 0), 1) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| stations| mean_count| variance| zeros| zero_pct| |--------:|----------:|--------:|-----:|--------:| | 800| 3.9| 22.78| 180| 22.5|
::: ::: ## Python ```python import pandas as pd from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_clean survey = load_coastal_survey_clean() pd.DataFrame({ "stations": [len(survey)], "mean_count": [round(survey["abundance"].mean(), 2)], "variance": [round(survey["abundance"].var(), 2)], "zeros": [int((survey["abundance"] == 0).sum())], "zero_pct": [round(100 * (survey["abundance"] == 0).mean(), 1)], }) ``` ::: Two features of that summary decide almost everything that follows. **The variance is far larger than the mean**, about 23 against 3.9. For a Poisson process they would be equal. This is *overdispersion*, and it is the normal condition of ecological count data: individuals cluster, so counts vary more than chance alone predicts. **Nearly a quarter of stations caught nothing.** A model that can only produce smooth positive numbers will never reproduce that spike at zero. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} p_count <- ggplot(survey, aes(abundance)) + geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = ml_palette[["blue"]]) + labs(x = "Individuals caught", y = "Stations", title = "As a count: regression") p_binary <- survey |> mutate(status = if_else(abundance > 0, "present", "absent")) |> count(status) |> ggplot(aes(status, n)) + geom_col(fill = ml_palette[["orange"]], width = 0.6) + geom_text(aes(label = n), vjust = -0.4, size = 4) + scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12))) + labs(x = NULL, y = "Stations", title = "As a category: classification") p_count + p_binary ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![One measurement, two questions. Left: the count, with a large spike at zero and a long right tail. Right: the same data reduced to presence and absence: simpler, and most of the information has been thrown away.](regression-and-classification_files/figure-html/fig-two-framings-1.png){#fig-two-framings fig-alt='Two panels. The left panel is a histogram of abundance with a tall bar at zero, a peak at one to three individuals and a long tail extending past thirty. The right panel is a two-bar chart of absent versus present, with present about three times taller than absent.' width=1700} ::: ::: ### The cost of dichotomising Turning the count into presence/absence is a real choice, and it is not free. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey |> filter(abundance > 0) |> summarise( `stations recorded as "present"` = n(), `smallest catch` = min(abundance), `largest catch` = max(abundance), `median catch` = median(abundance) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| stations recorded as "present"| smallest catch| largest catch| median catch| |------------------------------:|--------------:|-------------:|------------:| | 620| 1| 40| 3|
::: ::: ## Python ```python caught = survey.loc[survey["abundance"] > 0, "abundance"] pd.DataFrame({ 'stations recorded as "present"': [len(caught)], "smallest catch": [caught.min()], "largest catch": [caught.max()], "median catch": [caught.median()], }) ``` ::: A station with one individual and a station with forty are both simply "present". If your question is where the species *occurs*, that is a legitimate simplification. If it is about where the species is *abundant*, you have just deleted the answer. The reverse mistake is more common and more damaging: taking a genuine quantity, choosing a cut-off, and modelling the category. "High" versus "low" chlorophyll at 1 mg m⁻³ throws away all the variation on both sides of the line, and puts 0.99 and 0.01 in the same box while separating 0.99 from 1.01. ::: {.callout-warning} Dichotomise only when the *decision* is genuinely binary: a threshold in regulation, a survey protocol that records occurrence. Never dichotomise to make a modelling problem easier. It is the one preprocessing step that reliably destroys information you cannot get back. ::: ## Three things that travel together The response type determines three things, and they travel together: | | Regression | Classification | | --- | --- | --- | | **Model** | `linear_reg()`, `poisson_reg()`, `rand_forest(mode = "regression")` | `logistic_reg()`, `rand_forest(mode = "classification")` | | **Minimises** | Squared error, or a likelihood suited to the response | Log-loss, or a related likelihood | | **Measured by** | RMSE, MAE, $R^2$ | Accuracy, ROC AUC, precision, recall | In tidymodels the change is often one argument, `set_mode("classification")`, which makes it easy to switch and easy to forget that you have changed the scientific question as well as the code. For our counts specifically, the summary above already rules things out. The response is discrete, non-negative, overdispersed and a quarter zeros. Ordinary linear regression assumes none of that, which is precisely why it produced negative predictions in [section 1](../01-introduction/prediction-and-explanation.qmd). The [next page](linear-and-polynomial-regression.qmd) fixes it. ## Limits of the two boxes **Counts are not really "just regression".** They need a model that knows the response is a non-negative integer with mean-dependent variance. Fitting a Gaussian model to counts is common, works acceptably when counts are large, and fails visibly when they are small, as here. **Many zeros may mean two processes.** A zero can mean "the species does not live here" or "it lives here and we missed it". Hurdle and zero-inflated models separate those, and they correspond to a real biological distinction between habitat suitability and detection. **Ordinal responses lose information both ways.** Treated as nominal, the order is thrown away; treated as a number, equal spacing is invented. Ordinal models exist and are underused. **Multi-class is not just binary repeated.** With twenty species, class imbalance, confusable pairs and the choice between one-versus-rest and one-versus-one all arrive at once. ::: {.callout-tip} ## Key points - Identify what kind of response you have before choosing anything else. It fixes the model, the loss function and the metrics. - Counts are regression, but not Gaussian regression: discrete, non-negative, and overdispersed. Here the variance is roughly six times the mean. - Check the proportion of zeros early. A quarter of our stations caught nothing, and no smooth positive model reproduces that. - Dichotomising a quantity destroys information permanently. Do it when the decision is genuinely binary, never to simplify the modelling. - Switching mode in tidymodels is one argument, which makes it easy to change the scientific question by accident. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Compute the mean and variance of `abundance` within each substrate type. Is overdispersion uniform, or concentrated in particular habitats? 2. Take `chlorophyll_mg_m3`, split it at its median into "high" and "low", and fit a classification model. Compare what you can say from it with what a regression on the raw value tells you. What was the cut-off worth?
